etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ina/ → /ija/ → /ije/ → /iːe/
First cited to the late 1600s.
Shift from いや (iya), from even earlier 否 (ina). While いや (iya) was broadly used in the Muromachi period, in the Edo period, いや (iya) shifted to use mainly in informal or more intimate contexts, while いいえ (īe) was used in more formal or polite contexts. いや (iya) is still in use, including broader senses not included for いいえ (īe).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Uncertain. Perhaps from Chinese 餛飩 /馄饨, or a blend of this term and 温(おん) (on, “warm”). Compare Japanese 餛飩.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The element にこ (niko) is onomatopoeic for smiling, and also seen in にこやか (nikoyaka, “smiling”) and にこり (nikori, “with a bright smile”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Internationalism; see English stereo.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 以 (i-, “from... and”) + 後 (go, “behind; after”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 住 (MC drjuH).
The goon pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From classical noun 勢(いきほ)ひ (ikifofi), 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 勢(いきほ)ふ (ikifofu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The くち (kuchi) element is 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth”). Several dictionaries, such as Kōjien gloss the meaning of this overall term as 口縁(くちべり) (kuchiberi), consisting of 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth”) + 縁(へり) (heri, “edge”). Therefore the current pronunciation kuchibiru may be a shift from an earlier kuchiberi. The h of heri now becomes a b in an instance of rendaku (連濁), but may not have in older Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 小(しょう)学(がく) (shōgaku, “elementary school”) + 生(せい) (-sei, “student; pupil”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 少(すこ)し (sukoshi) + も (mo), literally "(not) even a little".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 強(つよ)い (tsuyoi, “strong”) + まる (-maru)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
First attested in c. 759 in the Man'yōshū.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Learned borrowing from Middle Chinese 文化 (mjun xwæH, “the way of educating by using morality, literature, rituals and music”), repurposed during the Meiji period as a translation of German Kultur.
Cited with the culture sense starting from roughly 1870.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Change in meaning from 枝(え) (e, historically ye, “branch, stem”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Used in the Kojiki. Generally regarded as cognate with 黴(かび) (kabi, “mold”), from the shared idea of sprouts or shoots. Appears to be the noun stem of Old Japanese verb かぶ (kabu) (source of modern 黴(かび)る (kabiru, “to go moldy”)), with probable original meaning of to sprout.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kabi/ → /kapi/ → /kaɸi/ → /kawi/ → /kai/
Alteration of kabi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kara. Origin of particle から (kara, “from, because”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
In light of the stem sense, probably derived semantically from origin, source meanings.
Compare also Korean 가락 (garak), similarly used as a counter for long and slender objects.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of kara, “qualities, characteristics”. Originally only found as a suffix. The kara changes to gara as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The rendaku pronunciation was then later used independently.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Cognate with 束(つか) (tsuka, ancient unit of length, equivalent to the amount covered from pinky to forefinger when gripping something; analogous to English hand).
Both likely derive from verb 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to set to, to attach, to accompany”), particularly as seen in modern Japanese idioms such as 手(て)を付(つ)ける (te o tsukeru, “to set one's hand to something”), 手(て)が付(つ)く (te ga tsuku, “to start using something”, literally “one's hand sets on something”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of verb 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to attach”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: やわらか (yawaraka, “soft, gentle”, na-adjective) + い (-i, suffix forming adjectives).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *asya.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 汗 (MC han|kan|hanH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720. Reconstructed as deriving from Proto-Japonic *minato.
The traditional etymology that Japanese sources trace back to is a compound of 水 (mi-, “water”) + な (na, assimilated apophonic form of の (no, “genitive case marker”)) + 門 (to, “gate”).
* However, this does not correlate cleanly with the etymology of 水 (mizu, “water”), reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *mentu (“water”). Then again, there are numerous attested words where 水 (mi) is used as the first and last element in compounds, suggesting either that the derivation of 水 (mizu) might differ.
Vovin, on the other hand suggests that the initial mi- was 御 (mi-, “honorific prefix”), while -na- meant "water", possibly from Proto-Tai *C̬.namꟲ (“water”). Compare 涙 (namida, “tears”), 菜葱, 水葱 (nagi, “Monochoria vaginalis”), 漬く (nazuku, “soak in water”, obsolete).
* However, this may present semantic difficulties, as any native formation like namida that proposes "water" for the initial nam and "eye" for a following component reverses the usual word-formation pattern for Japanese, where the main or head noun comes last. In addition, the na element appears in other words with no relation to "water", as an assimilated apophonic form of genitive particle の (no), seen in terms such as 掌 (tanagokoro, “palm of the hand”, literally “hand's heart/center”), 眼間 (manakai, “where the lines of sight of the eyes converge”, literally “eyes' exchanging/crossing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Of 特(とく) (toku, “special”, noun) plus に (ni, particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) + 黒 (kuro, “black”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 社会 (shakai, “society”) + 科学 (kagaku, “science”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 花 (hana, “flower”) + 見 (mi, “seeing, viewing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
薄(うす) (usu, root of 薄(うす)い (usui, “thin, dilute”)) + める (-meru, “-ify, -en”), developed from Classical Japanese 薄(うす)む (usumu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 衛 (ei, “to guard”) + 星 (-sei, “celestial body”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 記事 /记事 (kiᴴ dzriᴴ, literally “record + affair, event”). Compare modern Mandarin reading jìshì.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: See 早い.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 勧(すす)める (susumeru) and 薦(すす)める (susumeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 銓衡／铨衡. 選考 is a daiyōji replacing 銓衡.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From classical form 重(かさ)ぬ (kasanu), from Old Japanese.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Likely derived from a mimetic word, via reduplication. Cognate with Okinawan 響ちゅん (fibichun).
